label: GPT-6.1 Sol
output:
Dear Kelechi,

You said if I was serious, I should put it in writing. So here we are. A proper letter, delivered by Royal Mail to Croydon, because apparently my voice notes no longer meet your professional standards. Please keep this somewhere safe. The postage alone should tell you I mean business.

I’ve been thinking about what you said at my birthday. Not just the usual complaints about work—we have been hearing about that spreadsheet for some time now—but how tired you sounded. Nine years at the same firm is no small thing. You’ve built a career, you know what you’re doing, and I’m not going to pretend that’s something you can just throw away because your friend had an idea between food and cake.

But I wasn’t joking when I said you should come and teach maths.

Before you start, I know. I’m a teacher recommending teaching. Very suspicious. Like somebody selling insurance at a wedding. But I’ve known you since Unilag, long before I had a classroom or you had strong opinions about other people’s costings. I’m saying this because I’ve seen you teach, even when you didn’t call it that.

Half of Moremi would have been in serious trouble before exams without you. You’d sit there explaining something for the fourth time while the rest of us were ready to abandon both the question and the degree. And somehow you never made the person asking feel foolish. You could tease somebody, make them laugh, then find another way to explain it until it clicked.

That is not a small thing, Kelechi. Plenty of people are good at maths. You got an A in further maths; we know, congratulations again. But being able to do something and being able to help somebody else understand it are two different skills. You have both.

Look at Christmas. My nephew still talks about those plates of jollof rice. We were trying to get him through fractions, and you quietly turned lunch into a lesson. Suddenly halves and quarters meant something because he could see who was getting which portion, and whether somebody was trying to cheat him. He understood it. More importantly, he stopped looking as if fractions were something invented to disgrace him personally.

You probably went home and forgot about it. He didn’t.

That’s why I’m writing, really. Not because I think every bored quantity surveyor should be issued a whiteboard pen. I think *you* could be good at this.

Now let me spoil the recruitment speech before you accuse me of hiding the evidence.

Teaching is hard. Properly hard. Some days the marking seems to reproduce in your bag on the journey home. Behaviour can be wahala. There are lessons you prepare carefully that still go badly, and afternoons when you hear your own name so many times you wish you had never been given one. Being patient and funny helps, but it doesn’t mean every child will listen or every day will feel worthwhile.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice that I’m admitting to in an official document, anyway. I remember sitting there trying to gather myself before driving home, wondering whether I had made a terrible mistake.

It got better. I learned. I got help. Things that had felt impossible became things I knew how to handle. I still have bad days, and I’m not writing to offer you a life without stress. You already know me too well for that nonsense.

But I want to tell you about Damola.

He’s in Year 11, and last month we spent three weeks trying to get simultaneous equations to make sense to him. Three weeks of explaining, practising, getting somewhere, then apparently returning to the beginning. I was frustrated. He was more frustrated. Then one day it landed.

He looked at his work, looked at me and shouted, “Is that all??”

As if I had deliberately been withholding the simple version for my own entertainment.

The whole class clapped. He was grinning. I was trying to carry on with the lesson as though I wasn’t ridiculously pleased. It wasn’t a grand occasion. Nobody outside that room knew anything had happened. But I went home happy that day.

I can so easily imagine you in that room. You’d have laughed at him first, obviously. Then you’d have given him another question to check he really understood.

Our school has about 1,100 kids, and two of our Year 9 maths groups have had a supply teacher covering them since September. I’m not telling you that to make you personally responsible for the staffing problems of south London. Those children are not an invoice I’m posting to your house. But there is a real need for people who know their subject and can explain it without making a child feel stupid. You would bring something useful.

There are practical things to think about, of course. The route I’m talking about is the salaried one: one year of training, starting in September 2027, with pay while you train. That does not make the money question disappear. You would take a pay drop in the first year, and I’m not going to wave that away with “but think of the fulfilment”. Fulfilment has yet to pay anybody’s council tax.

You’d need to look at the actual figures and decide what you could manage. There’s the pension to consider, the holidays, and pay progression afterwards. And yes, before you say it, teachers do work during the holidays. You have watched me marking often enough to know that. Still, having those breaks is something I value. It’s worth looking at the whole picture rather than ruling it out on the first number.

Also, you are 34. Please don’t begin behaving as if you’ve missed the last bus. A woman in my department started at 41. Your nine years of working life would come with you; you wouldn’t have to leave them at reception. You know what maths is used for beyond passing an exam. You know how to work with people, meet deadlines and keep going when something is tedious. I suspect you’ve had extensive practice at that last one.

On your birthday, you said, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.”

I remember it. I’m not going to use your own sentence to bully you into a new career. Your work now matters too, even if you’re fed up with it. But I do wonder whether checking other people’s costings is giving enough room to the part of you that comes alive when you’re helping somebody understand something.

So here is my actual request. No resignation letter. No dramatic announcement. No signing anything.

Come to the open evening at the training partnership in Lewisham on **Thursday 19 November 2026, at 6pm**. I’ll go with you.

Applications for next September open soon, so this is a sensible time to ask questions. Ask about the salary, the workload, the training and the support. Ask the awkward questions. You’re good at those. Then we can get something to eat afterwards, and you can tell me which parts sounded convincing and which parts sounded like rubbish.

If you come away knowing it isn’t for you, fair enough. At least you’ll have looked properly. That is all I’m asking.

You challenged me to put it in writing. I have now bought a stamp and everything. The least you can do is come to Lewisham.

Your friend,

P.S. You are absolutely allowed to bring a spreadsheet to compare the finances. I’m trying to find you a different job, not change your entire personality.
